tier_reason: Linux-Clang.md compares Jsonifier, Glaze and simdjson ondemand, with a row for each library in every read test. The benchmark code is public: Json-Performance source/main.cpp, include/tests.hpp and include/common.hpp, built by CMakeLists.txt. The page states Clang 24.0.0 and the i9-14900KF CPU, and CMakeLists.txt gives the flags (-O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -fomit-frame-pointer -flto=thin -finline-functions, lld), so this is Tier A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Small-value tests. Each value in the file is parsed as its own tiny document (e.g. [START]true[END]). Double Test Read: 1345.06 vs simdjson 270.869 MB/s (~5.0x). Bool Test Read: 3090.41 vs 225.22 MB/s (~13.7x). String Test Read: 3881.15 vs 1591.5 MB/s (~2.4x). Uint64 Test Read: 2221.44 vs 637.965 MB/s (~3.5x). Whole-document reads are closer. Twitter (Minified): 2115.62 vs 1212.07 MB/s (~1.75x). CitmCatalog (Minified): 1816.6 vs 1050.96 MB/s (~1.73x). Canada (Minified): 866.14 vs 633.802 MB/s (~1.37x). The page marks Twitter, Google Maps and Random (Prettified) as statistical ties with simdjson. Jsonifier loses Mesh (Prettified): 1918.85 vs simdjson 2113.31 MB/s (derived from page data)
corrections.workload: Read (parse into typed C++ structs, with UTF-8 validation on for all libraries) throughput against simdjson ondemand. Glaze is the only library compared on write. Tests: small-value files where each value is parsed as a separate tiny document (Double/Uint64/Int64/Bool/String), plus whole documents (Twitter, CitmCatalog, Canada, Discord, Google Maps, Instruments, Marine IK, Mesh, Random, minified and prettified). Measured by the adaptive-sampling BenchmarkSuite harness (commit 49d7727), pinned to Jsonifier 9b1cd1d, Glaze 76db773 and simdjson 6913ee1
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Clang 24.0.0, Release. From Json-Performance CMakeLists.txt: -std=c++23 -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -fomit-frame-pointer -flto=thin -finline-functions -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections, linked with lld (-Wl,-O2 --gc-sections). simdjson is built with SIMDJSON_DEVELOPMENT_CHECKS OFF and UTF-8 validation on. Jsonifier uses its AVX2 backend and simdjson uses haswell
corrections.hardware: Intel Core i9-14900KF (the page prints 'i9-14900KF-AVX2'), running under WSL2 (Linux 6.18.40.1-microsoft-standard-WSL2)
corrections.caveats: Run and published by the Jsonifier authors in their companion repo (Json-Performance), not by an independent party. The largest gains vs simdjson (5-14x) come from small-value tests that parse thousands of tiny single-value documents, where simdjson ondemand's per-document iterate() setup cost dominates. On whole documents the gain is ~1.1-1.8x, several tests are statistical ties, and simdjson wins Mesh (Prettified). The Marine IK Reverse tests deliberately read keys out of order, which is a known worst case for ondemand. The run was on WSL2 with a Clang 24 development snapshot and pinned to commits dated 2026-09-23, so results may shift with later commits

notes: All four quoted figures match the simdjson rows exactly. I added the whole-document range because the quoted tests are the most favorable microbenchmarks. Metadata checks out: MIT, 103 stars, not a fork, not archived, last commit 2026-09-24. The README also links an independent suite (Loki-Astari/JsonBenchmark), which I did not open.

tier_reason: In the 'Native — Go' table of RESULTS.md, jsoniter and encoding/json both run the same typed-struct decode plus reduce harness. The code is public: golang/bench.go, golang/decoders.go (jsoniter.ConfigCompatibleWithStandardLibrary vs encoding/json Unmarshal) and golang/parser.go, with the Makefile using plain `go build`. RESULTS.md and results.json state the i7-6820HQ CPU. golang/go.mod pins go 1.27.1 as the minimum toolchain, so Tier A. The exact Go patch release is not recorded.

corrections.workload: Unmarshal of 5 real SEC companyfacts JSON files (39.9 MB, 285,469 fact records) into typed Go structs, followed by the same fact filter, dedup and sum reduction. Timed over 20 passes after 2 warmups at 1/2/4/8 threads (file-level sharding). Every variant must return kept=245741. Run in the independent tegridy-benchie multi-language shootout
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Go gc toolchain: golang/go.mod declares `go 1.27.1` (minimum toolchain; the exact version is not recorded). Built with plain `go build` (GOFLAGS=-mod=mod, default flags) per the Makefile. Uses jsoniter v1.1.12 with ConfigCompatibleWithStandardLibrary
corrections.caveats: The repository was archived by its owner. The last code commit is 2022-09-15, and 2024-05-27 is only the archive/push date. The figure comes from a third-party shootout, not the project's own old benchmarks. That shootout is a new, 0-star repo (created 2026-09-23) with one run on one laptop CPU. The timed passes include the shared reduction work, so the ratio understates the pure-decode difference. In the same table, jsoniter is slower than sonic and goccy/go-json at every thread count. At 1 thread it is 0.87x the goccy baseline.

notes: The quoted numbers are all in jsoniter's own rows: 233.6 vs 128.8 MB/s at 8t and 79.3 vs 44.5 MB/s at 1t. At 2t it is 128.0 vs 73.4 and at 4t 171.4 vs 100.7, so the gain is a consistent ~1.7-1.8x. The metadata is correct apart from last_commit (MIT, 13,867 stars, archived). The Go toolchain is known only as >=1.27.1 from go.mod. If exact compiler versions are strictly required for Tier A, treat this as C.

tier_reason: Tier A applies only to the i7-1260P run. Its screenshot shows gcc (Debian 14.2.0-19) 14.2.0. The README states -O2 with default options and gives the CPU model. The benchmark code is public: json_test.c (LJSON modes 1-7) and benchmark/rapidjson_test.c, run by the README's test script. The ARM Cortex-A53 and i7-10700 runs give no compiler version.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README headline figures are best-case single files ('最快可达' = 'up to' in README_zh-cn): 'parses 131% faster and prints 147% faster than RapidJSON' on Cortex-A53 (twitter.jsonx10: RapidJSON parse 178 vs LJSON reuse mode 77 ms, unformatted print 109 vs 44 ms); 'parses 75% faster and prints 133% faster' on i7-10700 (twitter.jsonx100 parse 138 vs 79 ms; canada.jsonx100 unformatted print 844 vs 362 ms). On i7-1260P the README says 'parses 166% faster and prints 215% faster' (without file I/O), but the published screenshot's best parse ratio is 1000xtwitter RapidJSON 864 vs LJSON mode 3 345 ms (~2.5x, 150% faster); the print figure matches (formatted 759 vs 241 ms, ~3.15x). On canada.json the parse gain is small: 64 vs 44 ms (A53), 477 vs 444 ms (i7-10700, x100), 333 vs 297 ms (i7-1260P, x100) (derived from page data)
corrections.workload: Single-shot, millisecond-resolution DOM parse and formatted/unformatted print timings on nativejson-benchmark files (canada, twitter, citm_catalog) and author-built concatenations (twitter x10/x100/x1000, canada x100, citm x1000). The best of LJSON's 7 modes (reuse and fast arena modes) is compared with RapidJSON's default Document::Parse plus Writer/PrettyWriter, and with cJSON and yyjson
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc/g++ -O2 with default options (README Note 1 and build commands; ljson is also built with -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections). gcc 14.2.0 (Debian 14.2.0-19) is shown only in the i7-1260P screenshot. Compiler versions for the Cortex-A53 and i7-10700 runs are not stated
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark run by the sole author on three of their own machines, two of them VMs, and not independently reproduced. Headline percentages are best-case files with LJSON's best arena/reuse mode. The Chinese README says 'up to', but the English README drops it. The i7-1260P parse figure (166%) could not be reproduced from its screenshot, where the best visible figure is ~150%. Timings are single runs at ms resolution. RapidJSON is built with default options (no SSE4.2/NEON, not in-situ). The 'with file reading and writing' label on the A53/i7-10700 claims does not fit the matching rows, which exclude file I/O. The author says numbers shift between releases

notes: Downgraded because the claim is overstated, not because of the tier. The quotes are verbatim from the English README, but they are best-case 'up to' figures, and the i7-1260P parse figure is not supported by the chart. The corrected claim uses the screenshot values. Metadata checks out: MIT, 28 stars, last commit 2026-07-25, active.
